q: time seem to speed up as we get older
why does time seem to go faster as we age
why does time speed up as we get older
why does time seem to speed up with age
why time flies when you get older
time goes faster as you age
why do we perceive time differently as we age
a: The feeling that time speeds up as we get older is a well-documented psychological phenomenon with several scientific explanations. The proportional theory suggests that each passing year represents a smaller fraction of our total life experience. For a 5-year-old, one year is 20% of their entire life, while for a 50-year-old, it's only 2%. This makes each year feel relatively shorter. The novelty theory states that our brains encode time based on the amount of new information we process. Children constantly encounter novel experiences, creating dense, rich memories that make time feel longer in retrospect. Adults fall into routines, processing less novel information, so fewer memories are formed and periods feel shorter when looked back on. Neurologically, the brain's dopamine levels and the speed of neural processing change with age, potentially affecting our internal clock. The brain's default mode network also becomes more activated with age, which is associated with mind-wandering and less focused attention on the present moment. Additionally, as we age, the neurotransmitter dopamine declines, which may affect the brain's ability to register new experiences as distinct events. The combination of less novelty, routine-driven lives, and neurological changes creates the subjective experience of time accelerating with age.
